newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's new Socialist leader emerges from shadows.
newsitem.headline: Spain's new Socialist leader emerges from shadows.

text.p: Following in the footsteps of one of Europe's most charismatic leaders would be a daunting task for any politician.
But Joaquin Almunia, the man elected to replace former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez as head of the Socialist party, says he is unshaken by the prospect.
"I'm not afraid of comparisons with Felipe," he told reporters shortly after being elected on Sunday.
But then Almunia is never easily rattled, his colleagues say.
Described as sensible and hardworking, the 49-year-old politician who has spent much of his career in Gonzalez' shadow admits he is no showman.
"I have a fear of physical heights but not of political heights, and I'm normally considered to be a calm and cool person even in the most delicate moments," he said.
While never considered an orator of Gonzalez' stature, he delivered a stirring acceptance speech on Sunday that brought cheering party members to their feet.
"With this fresh start we must once again grasp the banner of change so that the future is better than the present, reviving the confidence in politicians," he said.

Socialists hope the short, balding Almunia will bring a fresh face to Spanish socialism and give the party the facelift it needs after losing last year's general election to Jose Maria Aznar's Popular Party.
"We're all confident he's the right person to revitalise the party and give it a fresh start ... He knows how the party works and he's got a consensus behind him," said a delegate from Valencia.
But whether Almunia will be the one to take the party into the next elections, scheduled for the year 2000, is not clear.
"We are going to work hard to win the next elections, although the candidate will be decided later," he told reporters.
A close friend of Gonzalez, Almunia is ideologically in tune with his predecessor and is believed to have been his first choice as successor.

Born in the northern Basque city of Bilbao where he studied law and economics, Almunia joined the Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) in the mid-1970s when Gonzalez was still in exile waiting for the fall of General Francisco Franco's military dictatorship.
With Franco dead, the Socialist party returned to Spain with Gonzalez at the helm, and Almunia became a parliamentary deputy for Madrid in 1979.

Almunia went on to serve as labour minister and later minister of public administration in the first Socialist administration which steered Spain on the path to democracy after almost 40 years of dictatorship.
More recently, Almunia became a prominent figure in the party as its parliamentary spokesman.

So it was no surprise when he found himself launched into a leadership battle when Gonzalez announced last week that he wa stepping down and called for a "change of generations" in the Socialist hierarchy.

After winning overwhelming approval from party members, Almunia declared the party more united than ever and pledged to return the Socialists to power in Spain as Lionel Jospin and Tony Blair have in France and Britain.
But when asked if his leadership approach would be akin to Jospin or Blair, he made clear he had his own ideas.
"My name is Almunia, of Arab origin, but unmistakenly Spanish," he said brusquely.
